1.pericope_label: Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people, saying, Thus saith the Lord, He that remaineth in this city shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence: but he that goeth forth to the Chaldeans shall live; for he shall have his life for a prey, and shall live. Thus saith the Lord, This city shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon’s army, which shall take it. Therefore the princes said unto the king, We beseech thee, let this man be put to death: for thus he weakeneth the hands of the men of war that remain in this city, and the hands of all the people, in speaking such words unto them: for this man seeketh not the welfare of this people, but the hurt. Then Zedekiah the king said, Behold, he is in your hand: for the king is not he that can do any thing against you. Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain how the confinement gave the prophet an audience, the court of the guard adjoining the palace so that soldiers on duty and people coming in could be spoken to, note the odd article in the phrase for the pit as the way to mark a definite one when the possessor's name cannot take it, and judge the pit deep enough to kill; Ellicott places Jucal from an earlier chapter and thinks him a Levite, connects the name Shephatiah with the royal house, warns against confusing this Gedaliah with the prophet's later protector, is candid that advice to desert sounded like treason to anyone not granting the divine commission and worse from a man lately arrested in what looked like desertion, sees a weak ruler yielding reluctant consent and finds the scene reminiscent of Pilate, takes the title son of the king for a court office, and reconstructs a cistern drained by the siege but holding feet of black stinking mud.

Gill finds nothing elsewhere about two of the four accusers and doubts the guess that one father is the priest named earlier, adds that court favours and the king's bread had not bought the prophet's silence while his confidence grew as the ruin neared, and weighs whether the king's phrase grants permission or states a fact about the princes' authority, preferring the first; Calvin makes the prison into a pulpit, since the prisoner was no less free than if he had walked the streets, points out that the same message had been fixed to the temple doors thirty years before so that nothing was new except the assumption that imprisonment had silenced him, calls the charge of weakening the soldiers' hands specious but empty, raises against himself the question whether a private man may urge subjects to break allegiance, rejects the reading that makes the king's answer a compliment to his counsellors, and holds up the world's cruelty and the servant's meekness together.

Clarke labels the four the faction hostile to the prophet, borrowing a scholar's name for an anti-theocratic party, says he never wavered nor equivocated, abandons commentary for reproach in addressing a king who respected the prophet, feared the cabal and sacrificed an innocent man to both, and states bluntly that they meant him stifled.

Henry sets out the offer inside the threat, that the city cannot be saved but each man may save himself by going out early and taking his life as spoil, and adds that it is better to submit to a rebuke of providence than contend with it.

outliers.claim: Raises against himself the question whether a private man may urge subjects to break their allegiance, conceding that in civil terms a prophet is a private person however public his commission.
Concedes that the advice sounded like plain treason to anyone who did not grant the divine commission, and worse from a man lately arrested in what looked like desertion.

7.pericope_label: Now when Ebed–melech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin; Ebed–melech went forth out of the king’s house, and spake to the king, saying, My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is: for there is no more bread in the city. Then the king commanded Ebed–melech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die. So Ebed–melech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah. And Ebed–melech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so. So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch argue from the added noun that the word means a eunuch literally rather than a court officer figuratively, meet the law against mutilation by noting the man was a foreigner already so when taken into service, locate the store of rags in a room beneath the treasury and derive the three words for them from roots meaning to drag, wear out and dissolve, gloss the idiom about the thirty men as under your direction, and reject the emendation that would read three; Ellicott thinks the name had hardened from a title into a proper name, traces Cushite servants in the household back perhaps to David, renders the clause about dying as a present, explains why help was otherwise impossible, calls the store the lumber-room, and finds in the padded ropes the clearest measure of the suffering.

Gill has the rescuer leave his apartments as soon as he heard, notes that the gate was a fit place and moment for laying a case before the king, and hears the speech as at once deferential and bold; Calvin draws the implicit moral that among all the counsellors of a circumcised nation the one man who resisted was an alien, insists the appeal was deliberate rather than a spasm of pity since the man left the palace on purpose and spoke publicly, catches the phrasing that the prisoner would die although nobody touched him, asks how a king who had just confessed he had no authority dared act at all and answers that the change was an overruling from above, notes the tenderness of the armpits, and defends the decision to return the prophet to custody rather than to liberty.

Clarke explains that the king sat in the gate because it was the ordinary place of audience and judgment, infers real standing at court and a humane spirit from the willingness to speak against so powerful a group, supposes force was expected against the princes, and doubts a wardrobe proper is meant since eastern kings kept theirs stocked for gifts, suggesting the discarded and the insect-ruined; Wesley agrees that the escort was to guard against opposition.

debates.question: Why thirty men for the rescue?

positions.position: Because force was expected to be needed against the princes.
The number is large for a stripped garrison, and the text may originally have read three.
The idiom means under your direction, and the arguments for reading three are invalid.

outliers.claim: Notes that the rescuer left the palace on purpose and spoke in the gate before an assembly, which shows deliberation rather than a spasm of pity.
Reads the padded ropes as the clearest measure of the suffering, a pit deep enough to need them and a body wasted enough that they had to be cushioned before it could bear them.

14.pericope_label: Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the third entry that is in the house of the Lord: and the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me. Then Jeremiah said unto Zedekiah, If I declare it unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death? and if I give thee counsel, wilt thou not hearken unto me? So Zedekiah the king sware secretly unto Jeremiah, saying, As the Lord liveth, that made us this soul, I will not put thee to death, neither will I give thee into the hand of these men that seek thy life. Then said Jeremiah unto Zedekiah, Thus saith the Lord, the God of hosts, the God of Israel; If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon’s princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire; and thou shalt live, and thine house: But if thou wilt not go forth to the king of Babylon’s princes, then shall this city be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand.

schools.summary: Ellicott knows an outside royal entry and a covered gallery joining palace to temple, finds this third entrance named nowhere else and supposes it led up from the lower city, wonders whether the chief eunuch's chamber was used and arranged by the man who had just pulled the prophet out, thinks the eunuch's counsel may have prompted the summons, reads the prophet's question as assuming the king had approved the recent cruelty, prefers the older versions in the second clause so that it states the king will not listen, judges the oath deliberately weightier than the plain form, and reads the double promise as an admission that separates the king from the men who wanted the prophet dead.

Gill has the king send for the prophet as soon as he was back in the court of the guard, puts the reluctance practically, that speaking could only endanger the speaker and do the hearer no good so terms were worth settling first, and supplies two reasons for the secrecy of the oath, the dignity of a king swearing to a subject and fear of the princes; Calvin explains that the king could not enter the sanctuary so the court is meant, states at full strength the objection that the prophet bargained for safety before speaking and answers it by distinguishing occasions when no express command to speak had been given, observes that nobody swears in advance not to take offence unless he expects to be offended, cannot settle whether a fresh command was given for so repeated a message, and explains the pairing of promise and threat by the unresponsiveness of hypocrites to sweetness.

Clarke notes that the formula swears by the living God as author of the life each man has, calls it very solemn and marks it as the earliest recorded instance of swearing by the soul, and identifies the officers to be surrendered to as the generals then returning to the siege after beating the Egyptians, their master away at Riblah.

Henry names the contradiction the scene turns on, a king who had lately handed the prophet to his enemies now consulting him in private, one man's convictions and corruptions pulling against each other, reads the choice of a temple approach as respect proper in a man about to ask a word from God, and would render the request as a word rather than a thing.

debates.question: Was the prophet right to secure his own safety before answering?

positions.position: The objection is real, but the prophets did not always carry an express command to speak, and where none had been given prudence was open to him.
Speaking could only endanger the speaker and do the hearer no good, so terms were worth settling first.
He had no new word to give and feared to provoke a king he took to have approved the recent cruelty.

outliers.claim: Marks the king's formula as the earliest recorded instance of the custom of swearing by the soul.
Observes that nobody swears in advance not to take offence unless he expects to be offended, so the oath concedes the substance of the answer before it is given.

19.pericope_label: And Zedekiah the king said unto Jeremiah, I am afraid of the Jews that are fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me. But Jeremiah said, They shall not deliver thee. Obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the Lord, which I speak unto thee: so it shall be well unto thee, and thy soul shall live. But if thou refuse to go forth, this is the word that the Lord hath shewed me: And, behold, all the women that are left in the king of Judah’s house shall be brought forth to the king of Babylon’s princes, and those women shall say, Thy friends have set thee on, and have prevailed against thee: thy feet are sunk in the mire, and they are turned away back. So they shall bring out all thy wives and thy children to the Chaldeans: and thou shalt not escape out of their hand, but shalt be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon: and thou shalt cause this city to be burned with fire. Then said Zedekiah unto Jeremiah, Let no man know of these words, and thou shalt not die. But if the princes hear that I have talked with thee, and they come unto thee, and say unto thee, Declare unto us now what thou hast said unto the king, hide it not from us, and we will not put thee to death; also what the king said unto thee: Then thou shalt say unto them, I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathan’s house, to die there. Then came all the princes unto Jeremiah, and asked him: and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded. So they left off speaking with him; for the matter was not perceived. So Jeremiah abode in the court of the prison until the day that Jerusalem was taken: and he was there when Jerusalem was taken.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the particular fear in character, since the deserters were the prophet's own followers acting on his advice and a king who had flinched at one man's taunts could not face their derision, suspects the fear went past mockery to mutilation, notes that the closing clause is probably to be read as a statement that the city shall burn while the marginal rendering makes the king himself the burner and so his own act to answer for, and sees the vacillation running to the last; Keil and Delitzsch note that what the king expected did happen.

Gill has the prophet guarantee that no such surrender would be made, takes the women for court ladies and concubines left after famine and deportation, notes that only sons and not daughters are mentioned when the capture is later described, observes that nothing in the king's reply approves the counsel so that the silence is itself the refusal, and closes on the prophet still in the court of the guard; Calvin turns the guarantee into an argument about providence and calls refusal after such assurance deliberate perverseness, explains the figure of the women as a part standing for the whole, judges that the fear proves belief and that trembling was chosen over ending the anxiety at a stroke, adds the pitiable detail of a ruler who could have surrendered but expected to be killed in a tumult by his own counsellors, and declines to commend the evasion he records.

Clarke reads an actual defection in the harem, younger childless women slipping out to the enemy officers and making the taunt themselves while wives of the first rank had no such welcome to expect, calls the cover story the truth and nothing but the truth though not the whole truth, and argues that the prophet was under no obligation to say anything that would set a weak king against powerful men or cost him his life; Wesley states the fear plainly, presses the irony that a man afraid of men's insults would meet women's, and traces their reproach to the priests and false prophets who had encouraged him.

debates.question: Was the prophet's evasive answer to the princes excusable?

positions.position: Yes: it was the truth though not the whole truth, nothing proposed would defile his conscience, and he owed no statement that would set a weak king against powerful men or cost him his life.
No: the main thing was concealed and the reason given was not the true one, so a partial truth does not wholly excuse it, however well the king's slavish fear explains it.

outliers.claim: Reads an actual defection in the harem, the younger and childless women having already slipped out to the enemy officers and made the taunt themselves.
Prefers the marginal rendering that makes the king himself the burner of the city, so that the destruction would be his own act to answer for.
